definitions.definition: In the Gītā: evenness of mind in success and failure (2.48), skill in action (2.50), and the disconnection from union with sorrow (6.23); also the discipline of action as distinct from sāṃkhya (3.3). In the Mokṣadharma, the path relying on direct perception and a Lord, as against Sāṃkhya (12.289.3–7).
Performing one's prescribed action without attachment to its fruit, as a discipline that frees from the bondage of action (BhG 2.47–48, 3.3–9); judged better than mere renunciation of action (5.2).
The path of knowledge of the Sāṃkhyas, one of the two ancient paths named at BhG 3.3; its culmination is steadfastness in knowledge of the self.
Serving the Lord with unswerving devotion, by which one passes beyond the guṇas and becomes fit for Brahman (BhG 14.26); the theme of ch. 12.
Exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to Nārāyaṇa-Vāsudeva, the highest dharma (Nārāyaṇīya).
Meditation as taught in BhG 6.10–32 (a firm seat, erect posture, gaze on the nose-tip, mind fixed on the self or the Lord) and 18.52; in the Mokṣadharma a fourfold dhyāna-yoga (12.188).
Action guided by the resolute understanding that is free from attachment to fruits (BhG 2.49–50); the Lord gives it to his loving devotees (10.10) and Arjuna is told to resort to it (18.57).
Repeated practice of bringing the mind back to the Lord; the second step of the ladder of BhG 12.9, and the 'yoga of practice' of 8.8.

literal: enumeration; the path of discriminating knowledge

definitions.definition: In the Gītā, the understanding (buddhi) concerning the self (2.39) and the path of knowledge of the Sāṃkhyas (3.3), said to be one with Yoga (5.4–5); in the Mokṣadharma, the system that enumerates twenty-four principles with the puruṣa as twenty-fifth and relies on the teaching of the śāstra (12.289.7; 12.294), proclaimed by Kapila (12.337.60).

notes: U05's definition (the epic usage); classical Sāṃkhya is defined by U09.

literal: action; ritual act; the deed and its result

definitions.definition: Action, which no embodied being can abandon (BhG 3.5, 18.11) and which binds only through attachment to its fruit (2.47); also the ritual act (3.14) and the deed that follows its doer 'as a calf finds its mother' (MBh 12.174.16).

cross_language.note: same word; the Buddhist sense (intention as action) is defined by the Buddhist units

definitions.definition: Inaction, which the wise see in action and whose presence in inaction they also see (BhG 4.18); attachment to inaction is forbidden (2.47).
Action of a contrary or forbidden kind, which must be understood along with action and inaction (BhG 4.17).

notes: Commentators differ: prohibited action (Śaṅkara) or the various kinds of action (others).

definitions.definition: Freedom from the binding power of action, not attained by abstaining from action (BhG 3.4) but, as supreme perfection (naiṣkarmya-siddhi), by an understanding unattached everywhere through renunciation (18.49).
Later name for the Gītā's teaching of acting without attachment and without desire for the fruit (BhG 2.47–48, 3.19, 18.23).

notes: The compound is a commentarial and later label; the Gītā speaks of abandoning attachment (saṅga) and the fruit (phala).

definitions.definition: Giving up the fruit of all actions — what the discerning call relinquishment (tyāga) (BhG 18.2, 18.11); the fourth and most accessible step of 12.11, praised above meditation in 12.12.

equivalents.note: BhG 18.2 defines tyāga as relinquishing the fruit of all actions

definitions.definition: The duty proper to one's own nature and station, better even when imperfect than another's dharma well performed (BhG 3.35, 18.47); for Arjuna, the kṣatriya's duty to fight a righteous war (2.31); worship of the Lord by one's own work leads to perfection (18.46). In the Vyādha Gītā, the inherited occupation of the meat-seller done rightly (3.198).
The dharma of another, which is 'fraught with fear' even when well performed (BhG 3.35, 18.47).

The person whose wisdom is established: content in the self, free of desire, passion, fear and anger, the senses withdrawn like a tortoise's limbs, awake where others sleep, in the brāhmī state (BhG 2.54–72).

equivalents.note: the Gītā's descriptions of the one of steady wisdom (ch. 2), the one beyond the guṇas (ch. 14) and the dear devotee (ch. 12) share many marks
the later term 'jīvanmukta' (liberated while living) is applied by Advaita commentators to the sthitaprajña; the Gītā itself does not use the word

definitions.definition: The sage of steady mind whom sorrow does not agitate (BhG 2.56); 'among sages I am Vyāsa' (10.37).

The body and the whole of prakṛti with its modifications — elements, ego, intellect, the unmanifest, the organs, the objects, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, consciousness and steadfastness (BhG 13.1, 13.5–6).

The one who knows the field (body); the Lord declares himself the knower in all fields (BhG 13.1–2); it illumines the field as the sun the world (13.33). In the Mokṣadharma, the knower is the twenty-fifth, distinct from yet joined to sattva like fish and water (12.294, 12.187.39).
Vāsudeva, the knower of the field whose self is without guṇas (Nārāyaṇīya 12.326.38).

equivalents.note: the knower of the field of ch. 13 and the puruṣa of 13.19–23 are the same principle described from the side of knowing and of experiencing

definitions.definition: The Lord's nature: the lower, eightfold prakṛti and the higher life-element (BhG 7.4–5); beginningless, the cause of effect, instrument and agency, from which the guṇas arise (13.19–20); all action is done by its guṇas (3.27); under the Lord's oversight it brings forth the world (9.10).
The Lord's eightfold divided nature: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and ego (BhG 7.4).
The Lord's higher nature that has become the life-element (jīvabhūtā), by which the world is upheld (BhG 7.5).

The beginningless principle that experiences pleasure and pain, seated in prakṛti and bound by attachment to the guṇas (BhG 13.19–21); the perishable and imperishable puruṣas are surpassed by the highest (15.16–18); in the Mokṣadharma the twenty-fifth principle, many according to the Sāṃkhya-Yoga thinkers, one in source according to the Nārāyaṇīya's close (12.338).
The Lord, beyond the perishable and higher than the imperishable, who enters and sustains the three worlds (BhG 15.16–18).
Nārāyaṇa, reached by the ekāntins; those on the 'fourth path' go to him (MBh 12.336.3).

The supreme person in the body — witness, permitter, supporter, experiencer, great Lord (BhG 13.22); the highest puruṣa (15.17); beginningless and without guṇas, it neither acts nor is tainted (13.31).
All beings, the perishable puruṣa (BhG 15.16); perishable existence is the adhibhūta (8.4).

The imperishable supreme Brahman (BhG 8.3), the goal entered by ascetics (8.11); the unchanging (kūṭastha) imperishable puruṣa (15.16), surpassed by the highest person (15.18); also the syllable (Oṃ, 'the one syllable', 8.13, 10.25).
The unchanging: epithet of the imperishable puruṣa (BhG 15.16) and of the unmanifest worshipped by some (12.3).

The three strands born of prakṛti — sattva, rajas and tamas — which bind the embodied one (BhG 14.5), act upon one another as the true agents (3.27–28), and classify faith, food, austerity, giving, knowledge, action, agent, intellect, steadfastness and happiness (chs. 17–18).

The luminous, stainless guṇa that binds by attachment to happiness and knowledge (BhG 14.6); its sign is the light of knowledge in all the gates of the body (14.11); in the Mokṣadharma also the intellect as distinct from the knower of the field (12.187.39; 12.240.21–22).
The guṇa of passion, arising from thirst and attachment, binding by attachment to action (BhG 14.7); desire and anger are born of it (3.37).
The guṇa born of ignorance, deluding all beings, binding by negligence, sloth and sleep (BhG 14.8).

One who neither hates nor longs for the guṇas' effects, sits as if indifferent knowing that the guṇas act, is the same in pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour, and has renounced all undertakings (BhG 14.22–25); reached by unswerving devotion (14.26).

literal: the realm of the three guṇas

definitions.definition: The domain of the three guṇas, which is the Vedas' domain; Arjuna is told to be free of it (BhG 2.45).
The Lord's coming into being age after age by his own māyā to protect the good, destroy evil-doers and establish dharma (BhG 4.6–8); the noun itself is not used in the Gītā.
The Lord's successive manifestations (prādurbhāva), foretold by Nārāyaṇa to Nārada (MBh 12.326.72–94).
The Nārāyaṇīya's word for the Lord's appearances: Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma Bhārgava, Rāma Dāśarathi, the appearance at Mathurā, and earlier the Swan and the Horse-headed one (12.326.72–94).

The Lord's sovereign form shown to Arjuna with the divine eye: the whole universe in one body, with countless faces, brighter than a thousand suns, devouring the warriors as Time (BhG ch. 11); seen only by undivided devotion (11.54).

The Lord's manifestations in the best of every class — Viṣṇu among the Ādityas, the sun among lights, Oṃ among words, japa among sacrifices, Kapila among the perfected — all sprung from a fragment of his splendour (BhG ch. 10).

notes: In yoga texts vibhūti also means yogic power; the Gītā's sense is the Lord's glory.

definitions.definition: The Lord dwelling in the heart of all beings, moving them by his māyā (BhG 18.61); the great Lord of beings who comes into being by his own māyā (4.6); in the Mokṣadharma, the Yoga thinkers' argument that without a Lord no one is freed (12.289.3).

The Lord's power: by his own māyā he comes into being (BhG 4.6); his divine māyā made of the guṇas is hard to cross except by taking refuge in him (7.14); by it he moves beings as if on a machine (18.61).

notes: Advaita commentators read māyā as the principle of appearance; the Vaiṣṇava commentators as the Lord's real power (prakṛti).

definitions.definition: The Lord's yoga-māyā by which he is veiled and not manifest to all (BhG 7.25).

literal: son of Vasudeva; the indwelling god

definitions.definition: Name of Kṛṣṇa; 'Vāsudeva is all' is the realization of the rare great soul (BhG 7.19); 'among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva' (10.37).
The supreme of the fourfold form, the knower of the field without guṇas, dwelling of all, entered by the liberated (MBh 12.326.38; 12.332.17).

equivalents.note: the Nārāyaṇīya identifies Vāsudeva as the knower of the field

definitions.definition: The supreme Lord of the Nārāyaṇīya, also present as the ṛṣi at Badarī; the culmination of every system of knowledge (MBh 12.337.63–67) and the goal of the ekāntins (12.336.3–4).
Named by Bhīṣma in his hymn to Kṛṣṇa (12.47) and as the one attained by the Sāṃkhya follower (12.290).
The Lord (Bhagavān), speaker of the Gītā ('śrībhagavān uvāca') and object of the Bhāgavatas' devotion; the Pañcarātra's whole knower is 'the Lord himself' (12.337.63).
A worshipper of Bhagavat (Vāsudeva); the Nārāyaṇīya says Sāṃkhyas together with Bhāgavatas enter Saṃkarṣaṇa on the path of liberation (12.332.16).

The embodied self, unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain (BhG 2.20); to be raised by the self, being its own friend or enemy (6.5–6); the Lord as the self in the heart of all beings (10.20).

cross_language.note: cognate form; the Buddhist units record the denial of a permanent self

definitions.definition: The self as dweller in the body, which passes through bodily stages and into new bodies as one changes clothes (BhG 2.13, 2.22, 2.30); bound in the body by the guṇas (14.5).

The living being: the Lord's higher nature has become the life-element (BhG 7.5), and an eternal portion of him becomes the jīva (15.7); the living self in the body whose existence Bhṛgu defends (MBh 12.175–185).
The jīva is Saṃkarṣaṇa, arising from Vāsudeva (Nārāyaṇīya 12.326.38).
The eternal portion of the Lord that becomes the living being (BhG 15.7); the fragment of his splendour from which every glory springs (10.41–42).

notes: Read as a real part or as an apparent part according to school (see dsp:souls-one-or-distinct).

literal: the vast; the absolute; the Veda

definitions.definition: The imperishable supreme (BhG 8.3), beginningless, neither being nor non-being (13.12), with hands and feet everywhere (13.13); also the Veda from which ritual action arises (3.15) and the prakṛti called 'great Brahman', the Lord's womb (14.3); 'na mama' is the eternal Brahman (MBh 12.13.4).
The goal reached by one established in the brāhmī state even at death (BhG 2.72) and by sages free of faults, delighting in the welfare of beings, for whom it lies near on every side (5.24–26).

equivalents.note: the Gītā's compound shares the word nirvāṇa with Buddhist usage; whether and how the meanings relate is disputed and each tradition defines its own term

definitions.definition: The state of the one of steady wisdom, attaining which one is not deluded (BhG 2.72).

The state of the yogin at peace who has become Brahman (BhG 5.24, 6.27); having become Brahman, serene, he attains supreme devotion (18.54); fitness for it (brahmabhūya) comes from devotion (14.26) and discipline (18.53).
The own nature (svabhāva) of the Imperishable (BhG 8.3); the knowledge of the self is the best of sciences (10.32).
Perishable existence (BhG 8.4).
The Puruṣa (BhG 8.4).
The Lord himself in the body (BhG 8.4).
The welfare and cohesion of the world, for whose sake the wise act unattached, as Janaka did (BhG 3.20, 3.25).
Gain and security, whose burden the Lord bears for those who worship him with undivided minds (BhG 9.22); Arjuna is told to be free of acquiring and keeping (niryogakṣema, 2.45).
Devotion to the Lord, by which he is known, seen and entered (BhG 11.54); supreme devotion is attained by one who has become Brahman (18.54), and by devotion one knows him in truth (18.55).
One-pointed devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to Nārāyaṇa, 'the one devoted solely, intent on Nārāyaṇa' (MBh 12.336).
Devotion directed to nothing else, by which the supreme person is won (BhG 8.22), the Lord seen in truth (11.54) and gain and security borne (9.22).
One devoted to the Lord; the four kinds of devotee (BhG 7.16) and the devotee dear to him (12.13–20); 'my devotee never perishes' (9.31).
The knower, the fourth and highest of the devotees, whom the Lord regards as his very self (BhG 7.16–18).
The rare one who knows 'Vāsudeva is all' (BhG 7.19); great souls resort to the divine nature and worship with undistracted minds (9.13).
Taking refuge in the Lord (prapad-): Arjuna 'has taken refuge' as a disciple (BhG 2.7); those who take refuge in the Lord cross his māyā (7.14); 'I take refuge in that primal person' (15.4).
Surrender to the Lord alone, who frees from all sins (BhG 18.66); in the Rāmāyaṇa, Vibhīṣaṇa's refuge (6.18.33).

equivalents.note: the Gītā uses the verb prapad- and 'śaraṇaṃ vraja'; later Śrīvaiṣṇava usage treats prapatti and śaraṇāgati as synonyms

definitions.definition: Going to the Lord alone as refuge ('mām ekaṃ śaraṇaṃ vraja', BhG 18.66; 'take refuge in him alone', 18.62); Rāma's vow to protect whoever seeks refuge (Rāmāyaṇa 6.18.33).
Surrendering one who has sought refuge is counted among the gravest sins (MBh 17.3.15).

Two senses: the serenity of mind of one who moves among objects free of attraction and aversion (BhG 2.64–65, 18.37); and the Lord's grace, by which one attains the eternal abode (18.56, 18.62), sees the universal form (11.47) and regains memory (18.73).
Evenness in success and failure, which is called yoga (BhG 2.48); equality toward friend and foe (6.9, 12.18).
The wise who see the same in a learned brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater (BhG 5.18); the yogin who sees the same everywhere (6.29) and the Lord equally present in all (13.27–28).

The one-syllabled Brahman to be uttered at death while remembering the Lord (BhG 8.13); the praṇava in all the Vedas (7.8); the first of the threefold designation 'oṃ tat sat' with which the expounders of Brahman begin their rites (17.23–24); 'among words I am the one syllable' (10.25).

notes: U05's definition (the Gītā usage); Oṃ in the Upaniṣads and mantra-śāstra is defined by U03 and U31.

definitions.definition: The threefold designation of Brahman by which the brāhmaṇas, Vedas and sacrifices were ordained; Oṃ begins the rites, 'tat' marks acts done without seeking fruit, 'sat' denotes reality, goodness and praiseworthy action (BhG 17.23–27).

Faith, threefold by the guṇas and according to one's inner being — 'a person is made of faith' (BhG 17.2–3); the one with faith gains knowledge (4.39); what is done without faith is 'asat' (17.28); the Lord makes each devotee's faith steady (7.21).
Austerity, threefold — of body, speech and mind (BhG 17.14–16) — and sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic (17.17–19); terrible austerities not enjoined by scripture, tormenting the body, are demonic (17.5–6).
Giving, sāttvic when given because it ought to be given, to one who makes no return, at the right place and time to a worthy recipient (BhG 17.20).
Food, which is threefold by the guṇas: life-giving, savoury and wholesome for the sāttvic; bitter, sour and burning for the rājasic; stale and impure for the tāmasic (BhG 17.7–10).

Sacrifice, action done for whose sake does not bind (BhG 3.9); the wheel of sacrifice between gods and men (3.10–16); widened to many kinds — of material things, austerity, yoga, study, knowledge, breath (4.25–30) — the sacrifice of knowledge being highest (4.33); inwardly, the seven priests of the senses offering into the fire within (Anugītā 14.20).

The sacrifice of knowledge, better than the sacrifice of material things (BhG 4.33); some worship the Lord with it (9.15); the study of the Gītā itself is worship by the sacrifice of knowledge (18.70).
Silent recitation, the best of sacrifices ('among sacrifices I am japa', BhG 10.25).

Relinquishing the fruit of all actions (BhG 18.2), threefold according to the guṇas (18.7–9); the embodied cannot give up all action, and so the one who gives up the fruit is the relinquisher (18.11); one of the 'three horses of Brahman' (MBh 11.7.19; 5.43.14).

Laying aside actions prompted by desire (BhG 18.2); mere renunciation of action does not bring perfection (3.4), and renunciation is hard without yoga (5.6); the true renouncer neither hates nor desires (5.3; 6.1).
The set of virtues — fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in knowledge and yoga, non-harm, truth, compassion and the rest — that leads to liberation (BhG 16.1–3, 16.5).
Hypocrisy, arrogance, pride, anger, harshness and ignorance, leading to bondage (BhG 16.4–5); its bearers deny truth, foundation and a Lord (16.8).

Desire, born of rajas, the all-devouring enemy that veils knowledge, seated in senses, mind and intellect (BhG 3.37–41); one of the three gates of hell (16.21); yet 'in beings I am desire not opposed to dharma' (7.11); born of intention (saṃkalpa), as Maṅki says (MBh 12.171.25).
Anger, born of desire (BhG 2.62), twin of desire from rajas (3.37), a gate of hell (16.21).
Greed, the third gate of hell (BhG 16.21); a sign of increased rajas (14.12).
Delusion born of anger (BhG 2.63) and of the pairs of opposites (7.27); destroyed by the teaching, as Arjuna declares (18.73).
Practice, which together with dispassion restrains the restless mind (BhG 6.35); a step of the devotional ladder (12.9).
Dispassion, which with practice restrains the mind (BhG 6.35); dispassion toward sense-objects is a mark of knowledge (13.8).

The senses, which carry off the mind (BhG 2.60, 2.67), are withdrawn like a tortoise's limbs (2.58), and are high but lower than mind (3.42); in the Anugītā they are among the seven priests of the inner sacrifice (14.20).

The mind, higher than the senses (BhG 3.42), restless and hard to restrain like the wind (6.34), the sixth with the senses drawn by the jīva (15.7); in the Nārāyaṇīya the liberated 'become mind' in Pradyumna (12.332.15).
The understanding, higher than mind (BhG 3.42); resolute and one in the yogin (2.41); its destruction follows loss of memory (2.63); threefold by the guṇas (18.29–32).

Ego, one of the eight constituents of the lower nature (BhG 7.4); the deluded by ego think 'I am the doer' (3.27); free of 'mine' and ego one attains peace (2.71); in the Nārāyaṇīya, Aniruddha is called ahaṃkāra (12.327.26).

literal: that which upholds; duty, right, law

definitions.definition: The upholding order and right conduct: its decline occasions the Lord's descent (BhG 4.7); one's own dharma is better than another's (3.35); it is subtle (MBh 8.49) and its truth hidden (vulgate Yakṣapraśna); from it come artha and kāma (18.5.49); non-cruelty is its highest form (3.297.55).

cross_language.note: cognate; the Buddhist senses are defined by the Buddhist units

definitions.definition: Non-violence, 'the highest dharma for all beings that breathe' (MBh 1.11.12; 13.116); a mark of knowledge (BhG 13.7) and of the divine endowment (16.2); the eternal dharma taught by Tulādhāra (12.253–256); yet the meat-seller teaches that no one lives without some harm (3.199).
The ekāntins are non-violent; worship without animal slaughter (MBh 12.336.58; 12.323–324).
Non-cruelty, named the highest dharma by Yudhiṣṭhira to the Yakṣa (MBh 3.297.55, 3.297.71) and by the meat-seller (3.203.41); the reason Yudhiṣṭhira will not abandon the dog (17.3.7).
Truth, root of all and higher than any state (Rāmāyaṇa 2.109.13); established in dharma (2.21.40); the highest vow (MBh 3.203.41); part of verbal austerity (BhG 17.15).
The duties of the king, taught by Bhīṣma in the Śāntiparvan (12.1–128) and by Rāma to Bharata (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100).
Conduct permitted when normal dharma cannot be kept, illustrated by Viśvāmitra in famine (MBh 12.139).
The teaching on liberation, title of the third part of Bhīṣma's instruction (MBh 12.168–353).
The science of rule by the rod, composed by Brahmā when the first age declined (MBh 12.59); one of the three sciences sustaining the world (3.149.31–33).
Dharma, artha and kāma, of which dharma is the root (MBh 18.5.49); each to be pursued at its time (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100).
Dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa, on all of which the epic claims to contain everything (MBh 1.56.33); for Prahlāda 'puruṣārtha' as human effort is denied as a cause (12.215.15).

Time: 'I am Time, the destroyer of worlds' (BhG 11.32); 'Time takes all and gives all' (Bali, MBh 12.217.25); time is the sixth with the five eternal elements (12.267); in the Gautamī story, Time points to karma (13.1).
The divine or fated factor, the fifth cause of action (BhG 18.14); which does not bear fruit without human effort, as a seed without a field (MBh 13.6.7).
Human effort, without which fate does not succeed (MBh 13.6.7); defended by Draupadī (3.28–33).
One's inherent nature: it is svabhāva that acts (BhG 5.14); the varṇa duties arise from it (18.41); for Prahlāda all states arise and cease by svabhāva (MBh 12.215.15).

The four classes, created by the Lord according to guṇa and action (BhG 4.13), their duties arising from their nature (18.41–44); Bhṛgu teaches that the whole world was of Brahman and came to varṇa-division by actions (MBh 12.181.10); conduct makes the brāhmaṇa (3.177.16).
The fourfold order created by the Lord according to the division of guṇas and actions (BhG 4.13).
The ancient dharmas of a family, whose destruction in war Arjuna fears (BhG 1.40).
The mixture of varṇas that Arjuna fears will follow the ruin of families (BhG 1.41) and that the Lord says would follow if he did not act (3.24).
The imperishable tree with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns, to be cut with the axe of non-attachment (BhG 15.1–4); 'among trees I am the aśvattha' (10.26).
The bright path of fire, light, day, the bright fortnight and the northern course, by which knowers of Brahman go to Brahman and do not return (BhG 8.24).

notes: U05's contribution (the Gītā's form of the Upaniṣadic doctrine).

definitions.definition: The dark path of smoke, night, the dark fortnight and the southern course, by which one reaches the lunar light and returns (BhG 8.25).
The six months of the northern course, part of the bright path (BhG 8.24); Bhīṣma holds his breath until it comes (MBh 6.114.89–98).

literal: the time of the end, the hour of death

definitions.definition: The hour of death, when the state remembered determines where one goes (BhG 8.5–6); being in the brāhmī state even then brings brahmanirvāṇa (2.72).
The one who falls away from yoga before perfection; he is not lost but reborn among the pure or in a family of yogins and continues (BhG 6.37–45).
The sage who wishes to ascend to yoga, for whom action is the means (BhG 6.3).

literal: one who has ascended to yoga

definitions.definition: One who has ascended to yoga, for whom quiescence is the means; attached neither to objects nor actions, having renounced all intentions (BhG 6.3–4).
Breath-restraint as a form of sacrifice: offering in-breath into out-breath and the reverse, restraining their courses (BhG 4.29); equalizing the breaths in the nostrils (5.27).

notes: The Gītā names no counts or retention durations.

definitions.definition: The (in-)breath, offered into apāna in breath-sacrifice (BhG 4.29), fixed between the brows (8.10) or in the head (8.12) at death; the Lord as vaiśvānara joined with prāṇa and apāna digests food (15.14).
The complementary breath to prāṇa in the Gītā's breath-sacrifice (BhG 4.29) and equalization (5.27).
The vow of celibacy of the meditator (BhG 6.14) and of those desiring the Imperishable (8.11); bodily austerity (17.14); Sanatsujāta's four quarters of brahmacarya (MBh 5.44).
The settled state in which the resolute understanding stands unmoving (BhG 2.44, 2.53), not attained by those attached to enjoyment and power.

notes: The Gītā's usage precedes and differs from the technical samādhi of the Yoga Sūtra.

definitions.definition: The single, resolute understanding of the yogin, contrasted with the many-branched minds of the irresolute (BhG 2.41, 2.44).
The pairs such as heat and cold, pleasure and pain, from which one should be free (BhG 2.45, 5.3); the delusion of opposites born of desire and aversion (7.27).

literal: contact of the senses with objects

definitions.definition: The contacts of senses and objects giving cold and heat, pleasure and pain, transient and to be endured (BhG 2.14).
Enduring the transient contacts that give pleasure and pain (BhG 2.14).
Arjuna's despondency on seeing his kin, which gives the first chapter its name (BhG 1.28–47).
The fault of pity or faint-heartedness that strikes Arjuna's nature (BhG 2.7).
Disciple; Arjuna declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple and asks to be taught (BhG 2.7).
Prostration before the wise, the first of the three ways to learn knowledge (BhG 4.34).
Inquiry put to the wise, the second way to learn knowledge (BhG 4.34).
Service of the wise, the third way to learn knowledge (BhG 4.34); the Lord is served with unswerving devotion (14.26).
The secret teaching: the ancient yoga (BhG 4.3), the royal secret (9.2), the most secret (15.20, 18.63–64), not to be told to the undisciplined or undevoted (18.67).
The royal knowledge and royal secret of ch. 9, supreme purifier, directly perceived and easy to practise (BhG 9.1–2).
The Lord's supreme abode, not illumined by sun, moon or fire, from which there is no return (BhG 15.6, 8.21).
Non-return to rebirth, reached by those who come to the Lord (BhG 8.15–16), by knowers who depart on the bright path (8.24), and by the knowers of the self (5.17).
The cosmic period at whose end beings enter the Lord's prakṛti and at whose beginning he sends them forth (BhG 9.7).

An age: the Lord comes into being age after age (BhG 4.8); Brahmā's day and night last a thousand ages each (8.17); the four ages and their decline taught by Hanumān (MBh 3.148) and Nārada (Rāmāyaṇa 7.74).
One devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, dwelling in the White Island or entering Vāsudeva directly without the intermediate goals (MBh 12.323.26; 12.336.3–4; 12.332.18).

The dharma of the ekāntins, the best and dear to Nārāyaṇa, equal to Sāṃkhya-yoga, by which one goes to the imperishable Hari (MBh 12.336.4, 12.336.69); sung by the Lord to Arjuna before the battle (12.336.8).
The ancient great dharma given by Nārāyaṇa at the beginning of the Kṛta age and upheld by the Sātvatas (MBh 12.336.27–51).

The system of Nārāyaṇa worship called Pañcarātra in the Nārāyaṇīya, 'this great upaniṣad made by Sāṃkhya-yoga' (12.326.100), whose whole knower is the Lord himself (12.337.63); one of the five systems of knowledge (12.337.59).

notes: U05's definition (the early usage); the Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās are covered by U08.

definitions.definition: The fourfold form (caturmūrti) of the Lord — Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha — each arising from the prior (MBh 12.326.68–69).

notes: The word 'vyūha' for the fourfold form is the later Pāñcarātra term; the Nārāyaṇīya speaks of the Lord's four forms (mūrti).

definitions.definition: The second form, Śeṣa, identified with the jīva (MBh 12.326.38, 12.326.68).

equivalents.note: the Nārāyaṇīya identifies Saṃkarṣaṇa with the jīva

definitions.definition: The third form, born from Saṃkarṣaṇa; the liberated, 'becoming mind', enter Pradyumna (MBh 12.326.68; 12.332.15).

equivalents.note: Pradyumna corresponds to the mind in the Nārāyaṇīya's ascent

definitions.definition: The fourth form, from whom Brahmā arises; called the great self and ahaṃkāra (MBh 12.326.69; 12.327.26).
The island north of the milk ocean where the white, one-pointed devotees dwell and where Nārāyaṇa reveals himself to Nārada (MBh 12.323.23–26; 12.321–326).
The twin seers born in Dharma's house who perform austerity at Badarī (MBh 12.332.19), identified in the epic with Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa.
A principle of the Sāṃkhya enumeration: twenty-four together with prakṛti, the twenty-fifth beyond them (MBh 12.294.42); listed in the field of BhG 13.5.

The unmanifest: from which beings emerge at Brahmā's day (BhG 8.18); another eternal unmanifest beyond it is the Imperishable (8.20); worshipped by some (12.1–5); in the Mokṣadharma the field, prakṛti (12.294.38).
'Great Brahman', the Lord's womb (BhG 14.3); in the Nārāyaṇīya Aniruddha is called the great self (12.327.26).
The twenty-fifth principle, the knower beyond the twenty-four; the unawakened self called 'the one awakening', which on knowing itself becomes alone (MBh 12.294.42–43).

equivalents.note: the twenty-fifth of the enumeration is the puruṣa

definitions.definition: The twenty-sixth, stainless, awakened, immeasurable and eternal, which ever knows the twenty-fifth and twenty-fourth; the twenty-fifth attains its state on awakening (MBh 12.296.7–12).

equivalents.note: the Mokṣadharma's twenty-sixth above the twenty-fifth parallels the Gītā's highest person above the perishable and imperishable

definitions.definition: The twenty-fifth as unawakened yet awakening (MBh 12.294.43; 12.296.3–10).
In the Vasiṣṭha–Karāla dialogue, the twenty-sixth, the ever-awakened (MBh 12.296.7, 12.296.11).

notes: U05's definition (the epic Sāṃkhya usage); the Buddhist sense is defined by the Buddhist units.

definitions.definition: The unmanifest (prakṛti), which does not awaken, and the self while it has not awakened (MBh 12.292–296).
The power gained by yoga, by which the yogin checks sense-objects as an elephant stems a current and enters other beings at will (MBh 12.289.23–24).
Holding the mind in concentration: 'established in yogic concentration' at death (BhG 8.12); the concentrations of the Mokṣadharma's yoga (12.289).
The five faults to be cut off in yoga: desire, anger, greed, fear and sleep (MBh 12.232.4; 12.266.14).
The round of death and rebirth, from whose ocean the Lord lifts his devotees (BhG 12.7); the forest of Vidura's parable (MBh 11.5–6).
The genre of the Mahābhārata, which calls itself a Veda of Kṛṣṇa (MBh 1.1.205).
The epic's claim to Vedic status: it calls itself the 'kārṣṇa veda' (MBh 1.1.205).
The Upaniṣads, the Brahma Sūtra and the Bhagavad Gītā, the three canonical sources of Vedānta; the Gītā counts as the smṛti source. BhG 13.4 refers to 'the words of the Brahma-sūtra'.

notes: A later Vedāntic term; the Gītā does not use it.

definitions.definition: The devoted wife, whose power humbles the angry Kauśika (MBh 3.196–197), whom Sāvitrī exemplifies (3.281), and whose dharma Anasūyā teaches Sītā (Rāmāyaṇa 2.117–119).
The epic verse, born, the Rāmāyaṇa says, from Vālmīki's grief (śoka) at the krauñca's death (Rāmāyaṇa 1.2.15–18).
A sacred ford; Vidura calls the self a river with sacred fords whose water is truth, in which one is purified (MBh 5.40.19).
The warrior's duty, for whom nothing is better than a righteous war (BhG 2.31); heroism and not fleeing in battle are born of his nature (18.43).
Steadfastness, threefold by the guṇas; the sāttvic holds mind, breath and senses by unswerving yoga (BhG 18.33–35).
The ascetic livelihood of gleaning grain left in the fields; the gleaner's gift outweighs a horse sacrifice (MBh 14.92–93) and a gleaning sage attains the highest (12.340–353).
Living like a python on whatever comes unsought, without striving (MBh 12.172).
Freedom from hope or expectation, 'the highest happiness', learned by Piṅgalā (MBh 12.168.52).
Thirst from which, with attachment, rajas arises (BhG 14.7).

cross_language.note: cognate; defined in the Buddhist units

definitions.definition: Heedfulness, declared by Sanatsujāta to be immortality (MBh 5.42.4); one of the three 'horses of Brahman' with self-restraint and renunciation (11.7.19; 5.43.14).

cross_language.note: cognate; the Dhammapada's 'appamādo amatapadaṃ' is recorded by the Buddhist units

definitions.definition: Heedlessness, which Sanatsujāta calls death (MBh 5.42.4); a mark of tamas (BhG 14.8, 14.13).
Silence, part of mental austerity (BhG 17.16) and mark of the dear devotee (12.19); 'of secrets I am silence' (10.38); for Sanatsujāta, the true muni's silence (MBh 5.42–43).
Self-restraint, a mark of the divine endowment (BhG 16.1) and one of the three 'horses of Brahman' (MBh 11.7.19); taught by the Haṃsa (12.288).
Forgiveness, 'the highest peace' (MBh 5.33.48) and 'the highest strength' (3.203.41); a mark of the dear devotee (BhG 12.13).
The fire of digestion that the Lord becomes in living bodies (BhG 15.14); the fire within whose seven tongues are the senses, mind and intellect (Anugītā 14.20).
The body, in which the self-controlled embodied one dwells neither acting nor causing action (BhG 5.13).
The Lord as witness (BhG 9.18); cf. the supreme person as 'upadraṣṭṛ', the one who looks on (13.22).
The supreme person in the body as witness (BhG 13.22).
The divine eye given by Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna to see the universal form (BhG 11.8) and by Vyāsa to Sañjaya to see the war (MBh 6.2).
